ops.new_text: Block-term tensor models offer one route to such a model. A block-term decomposition splits a multiway signal into blocks with low-rank factors per mode \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. In neural networks, block-term structure has compressed weight matrices, and those networks are explained with Grad-CAM maps instead of through their factors \cite{arxiv_2010_04963}. In supervised regression of brain signals, block-term tensor regression, designed for interpretability, predicted finger movements \cite{Faes_2024}. That regression is linear and has no survival objective, which incident prediction with censored follow-up needs. To our knowledge, no published model places readable block-term frequency and lead factors on the predictive path of a survival network for incident AF. Such a model would also need a way to add clinical risk factors, which complement the ECG \cite{Khurshid_2022}. The clinical factors should not enter the factors that are meant to be read, or the reading would mix the two sources.

ops.new_text:
The contributions of the study are these:
\begin{itemize}
\item BTTN, a survival network whose ECG evidence passes through per-block frequency and lead factors, with a separate linear clinical term that does not pass through those factors.
\item An incident-AF cohort in MIMIC-IV-ECG defined from ICD-coded hospital diagnoses with a 30-day blanking window, reported with its exclusion counts.
\item A comparison of one-year discrimination against a clinical model, a CNN and linear block-term tensor regression (BTTR) under one protocol, and the discrimination of BTTN at four horizons, with BTTN fitted once as a survival model.
\item The calibration, risk stratification and operating points of BTTN with the clinical term.
\item A beat-aligned, energy-normalised occlusion profile of the ECG term of BTTN.
\end{itemize}

ops.new_text: A block-term decomposition writes a tensor as a sum of blocks of low multilinear rank, and it contains the CP and Tucker decompositions as special cases \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. A survey covers the CP and Tucker decompositions \cite{Kolda_2009}. The uses of block-term structure differ in where the factors sit: in the weights of a network, within a recording, or on the input of a predictive model. Block-term tensor neural networks approximate the weight matrices of CNNs and recurrent networks by block-term tensors to compress them, and the networks are explained with Grad-CAM maps instead of through their factors \cite{arxiv_2010_04963}. The model of this paper shares part of that name and is a different model, whose factors act on the input and can be read. On AF ECGs, a regularised block-term decomposition extracted several signals interpretable as AF patterns \cite{Goulart_2020}. That work separates sources within a recording and does not predict risk.

ops.new_text: Occlusion sensitivity covers part of the input and records the change in the output \cite{Zeiler_2014}. It is one of the perturbation-based explanation methods \cite{Ivanovs_2021}. We applied it to a single ECG-only BTTN trained on the whole survival sample. For the 120 highest-risk ECGs of patients with an event, a window of 12 samples (24 ms at 500 Hz) was set to zero in every beat of one lead. The window ran from 6 samples before to 5 samples after a fixed offset from each R peak. Each offset was rounded to a whole sample towards the R peak. R peaks were detected on lead II. The spectrogram was rebuilt and the drop in log-risk recorded, for each lead and for offsets from 350 ms before to 425 ms after the R peak in steps of 25 ms. Neighbouring windows abut or leave one sample between them. Zeroing a high-energy part of the beat changes the spectrogram most. Each mean drop was therefore also divided by the sum of two terms: the mean energy of the removed samples, and, for stability, one tenth of that energy's mean over all leads and offsets.

ops.new_text: In the one-year design, the fused model had the highest AUROC of the methods compared, 0.7776 (95\% CI [0.7664, 0.7888]) (Table~\ref{tab:oneyear}). Its interval lay above the CNN's interval of [0.7226, 0.7469]. It overlapped the interval of the clinical model, 0.7597 [0.7488, 0.7713], and the study reports no paired interval for this difference. The two estimates are therefore reported side by side. ECG-only BTTN reached 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517] and the CNN 0.7350, with overlapping intervals, so the two are comparable on this cohort. ECG-only BTTN exceeded linear BTTR, at 0.5967 [0.5824, 0.6115], with intervals that do not overlap.

ops.new_text: Fitted once in the survival design, the fused model had an AUROC of 0.723 [0.701, 0.745] at 120 days, for onset in the 90 days after the blanking window, 31 to 120 days after the index ECG (Table~\ref{tab:horizons}). Its AUROC was 0.727 [0.711, 0.743] at one year, 0.740 [0.727, 0.753] at two years and 0.745 [0.735, 0.755] at five years. The clinical Cox model had point estimates of 0.710, 0.711, 0.727 and 0.731, below those of the fused model at each horizon. ECG-only BTTN ranged from 0.658 to 0.676. The four horizons share one model and overlapping patients. They describe the behaviour of one model and are not independent replications. One reason for the lower one-year values of the survival design is its control group. At one year it includes patients who develop AF later, whereas the controls of the one-year design have no AF diagnosis.

ops.new_text: After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model were close in most deciles, among 19,986 patients with 838 cases (Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}). The largest gap lay in the sixth decile (bar 5 of Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}), 4.95\% observed against a mean prediction of 3.56\%. The deciles are read in the survival sample, which holds a larger share of the events of the cohort than of its controls (4,000 of 8,775 against 16,000 of 41,770). Its proportions of AF are therefore higher than those of the cohort. Observed one-year AF rose from 0.55\% in the lowest decile to 11.4\% in the highest, with mean predicted risks of 0.61\% and 12.3\%. The sixth decile also had a higher observed proportion than the seventh (bar 6, 4.15\%). Brier scores were 0.0390 for the fused model, 0.0396 for ECG-only BTTN and 0.0398 for the clinical model.

ops.new_text: These results answer the research question within one health system. BTTN with the clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its point estimates stayed above those of the clinical model at four horizons read from one survival model. Its ECG term alone was comparable to a CNN under the same protocol. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed closely in most risk deciles. It flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Per unit of energy, its ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. The gain of the fused model over the clinical model is small and consistent in direction. The one-year intervals overlap, and the study reports no interval of the difference that would establish it.

ops.new_text: Separating the clinical term from the block-term layer lets the fused model gain discrimination without passing the risk factors through its ECG factors. The ECG evidence still passes through frequency and lead factors, and each risk factor enters the linear term with one weight. The two sources therefore have separate parameters that can be inspected apart, although this study reports no reading of the fitted frequency and lead factors. The fused model is trained as one network, so its factors are fitted beside the clinical term and may differ from those of ECG-only BTTN. In a fused network whose clinical inputs enter the factor layer, the factors could absorb risk-factor information, as concept representations absorb information beyond their concepts \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The architecture of BTTN closes this route for the clinical term. It does not close it for information that the ECG itself carries, which the factors may encode in ways a reader does not expect.

ops.new_text: On ICD-coded hospital diagnoses linked to MIMIC-IV-ECG, a block-term tensor network with a separate clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its AUROC was 0.7776, against 0.7597 for a clinical model and 0.7350 for a CNN. Fitted once as a survival model, it kept its point estimates above those of the clinical model at horizons from 120 days to five years after the index ECG. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed closely in most risk deciles. The fused model also flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Its gain over the clinical model is small, and the one-year intervals overlap. The gain is consistent in direction within one health system, and no interval for the difference yet establishes it.

ops.new_text: The ECG term alone reached the discrimination of a compact CNN under the same protocol, while its evidence passes through frequency and lead factors that lie on the predictive path and can be read. The clinical term adds the risk factors without passing through those factors. Per unit of signal energy, the ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. This is the part of the cardiac cycle that cohort studies of the PR interval tie to later AF \cite{Cheng_2009,Magnani_2013}. The readout describes the fitted model, and its atrial reading remains a hypothesis.

ops.new_text: For the design of ECG risk models, the results suggest that clinical factors can be added beside block-term factors without entering them. The clinical comparator used here is narrower than a full clinical score, and the readout is descriptive. Validation outside one health system, a test of the factors on ICD-coded labels and a comparator that includes the PR interval are the next requirements before any clinical use.
